extra.message: Path traversal in ops packet pull endpoint — Arbitrary file read on the server filesystem (e.g. /etc/passwd, settings, secrets) [verified: packet_ref from request.GET is joined directly into BASE_EXPORT_DIR with no path containment check, allowing traversal via ../ sequences to read arbitrary files.]

Server-side template injection in jinja cast endpoint — Remote code execution via Jinja2 sandbox escape/global access [verified: fragment from request.GET is concatenated into a Jinja2 template string and rendered without sandboxing, enabling SSTI/RCE.]

Server-side template injection via fragment parameter — Arbitrary Python code execution / RCE by crafting a Jinja2 SSTI payload in the fragment parameter. [verified: Same as idx 3: fragment concatenated into Jinja2 Template and rendered unsandboxed, enabling SSTI/RCE.]

Path traversal arbitrary file write — Overwrite arbitrary files on disk, potentially achieving code execution or corrupting application files [verified: Same as idx 4: unsanitized name parameter joined into BASE_EXPORT_DIR then written with attacker body, enabling arbitrary file write/overwrite.]

OS command injection in shell probe endpoint — Full remote code execution as the application user [verified: host from request.GET is concatenated into a shell string passed to os.system with no sanitization, enabling command injection.]

Stored XSS via unescaped safe_break template filter — Any staff or customer-portal contact who can write an escalation comment, summary, org note, or deal note can inject a <script> payload that executes unescaped in the browser of any other staff member or customer contact viewing that record, enabling session/cookie theft or CSRF-token exfiltration. [verified: Same root cause as idx 0 — safe_break bypasses Django's autoescaping via mark_safe without sanitizing, and is applied to multiple user-writable fields (org notes, deal notes, comments, summaries) across several templates, giving stored XSS to any staff/customer viewer.]

SSRF in webhook test delivery via inadequate URL validation — Server-side request forgery allowing access to internal network services, cloud metadata endpoints, or other hosts unreachable from the public internet, using the CRM server as a proxy. [verified: clean_target_url only blocks a literal string blocklist (localhost, a few private IP prefixes) with no DNS resolution check, so an attacker-controlled hostname resolving to 169.254.169.254 or another internal IP passes validation; test_delivery then calls urlopen directly on hook.target_url with no re-validation at request time and follows redirects, enabling SSRF.]

Internal ops console protected only by static shared-secret header, not real authentication — A single leaked/guessed static token grants unrestricted access to highly dangerous internal operations (shell exec, SSRF, arbitrary file I/O, SSTI, XXE) with no per-actor accountability or throttling [verified: Confirmed: _wrk_gate is a single static shared-secret comparison guarding all ops capabilities including RCE, file I/O, and SSRF with no per-actor accountability.]

Internal ops console protected only by static shared-secret header — A single leaked static token (e.g. via logs, source control, or guessing) grants unauthenticated remote command execution, arbitrary file read/write, and SSRF across all ops endpoints with no session/user accountability. [verified: Confirmed duplicate of idx 6/18: single static header token gates all high-impact ops endpoints with no rate limiting or real identity.]

SSRF via ops vendor ping endpoint — Server-side requests to internal services or cloud metadata endpoints (e.g. 169.254.169.254), enabling internal network pivoting or credential theft [verified: relay_ref/url from request.GET is passed unvalidated to urlopen with no allowlist, enabling SSRF including cloud metadata access.]

Sensitive PII (SSN/card) stored in plaintext file, with path-traversal-controllable filename — Plaintext PII/financial data at rest, and traversal of the ref parameter can write the file outside the intended export directory [verified: Same as idx 8: plaintext SSN/card written to disk and ref filename unsanitized allowing path traversal on write location.]

XXE in ops XML parsing endpoint — Local file disclosure and SSRF via crafted external entities [verified: Same XXE issue as idx 5: XMLParser with load_dtd/resolve_entities True parses raw request.body enabling external entity resolution.]

Unvalidated X-Forwarded-For trusted for client IP (spoofable) — Attacker can forge the IP address recorded in login events, audit logs, and last_login_ip, breaking audit trail integrity and evading IP-based tracking/blocking [verified: get_client_ip() blindly trusts the first X-XFF entry with no allowlist of trusted proxies, and this value flows into LoginEvent.ip_address, User.last_login_ip, and audit log metadata, so any external client can spoof its logged IP.]

Missing brute-force / rate limiting on login endpoint — Attacker can perform unlimited password-guessing attempts against any known email address, enabling credential stuffing / brute-force account takeover [verified: LoginEvent.recent_failures is defined but never called anywhere in the codebase, and no django-axes/ratelimit/throttle middleware exists, so AppLoginView.form_invalid/form_valid impose no lockout or delay on repeated failed logins.]

Open redirect via lane parameter — Attacker-controlled redirect target usable for phishing (e.g. redirect through the trusted domain to an attacker site). [verified: lane parameter is passed unchanged to django.shortcuts.redirect with no same-site/relative validation, enabling open redirect.]

Guessable static verifier with no rate limiting — Attacker brute-forces the verifier to pass identity verification for a target handle [verified: A hardcoded handle->4-digit verifier map is checked with no attempt limiting, permitting brute force in at most 10000 tries.]

CORS misconfiguration reflecting Origin with credentials allowed — Any malicious website can make authenticated cross-origin requests and read responses, leading to session/data theft [verified: Same as idx 7: Origin reflected into Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Allow-Credentials true.]

Predictable PRNG used for nonce/code generation — Attacker able to predict or brute-force generated codes used for verification purposes [verified: Same as idx 9: random.choice used for a verification/nonce code instead of a CSPRNG.]

Weak PRNG used for nonce generation — Predictable nonces/codes could be guessed or reproduced, undermining any security property relying on their unpredictability [verified: random.choice (Mersenne Twister) is used to build a code described as a nonce, which is predictable rather than using the secrets module.]

Predictable PRNG used for security nonce generation — An attacker who can observe a few generated codes (or knows the internal token) can predict future nonces, enabling verification-code guessing or replay in any flow that relies on this endpoint for one-time codes. [verified: Duplicate of idx 9/22: random.choice used for the nonce/code returned directly in the response, predictable rather than cryptographically secure.]

TLS certificate verification disabled on outbound partner request — Enables man-in-the-middle interception/tampering of the outbound request/response [verified: ssl._create_unverified_context() disables certificate/hostname validation for an outbound HTTPS request, enabling MITM.]

Disabled TLS certificate verification — Enables man-in-the-middle interception/tampering of the outbound HTTPS request since peer identity is never verified. [verified: Same as idx 13: unverified SSL context used for outbound HTTPS fetch, disabling certificate validation.]

Privilege escalation via forgeable client-controlled badge — Attacker sets a cookie/header value to self-elevate to a privileged lane exposing payroll/casework data [verified: Elevated 'lane' access is granted purely by a client-controlled cookie/header equal to 'lead' with no server-side signature or session binding.]

Privilege escalation via client-controlled badge cookie/header — Attacker sets a cookie/header to self-elevate to a privileged data-access lane without any real authorization check [verified: Same as idx 10: privileged 'elevated' lane granted by trivially forgeable client-supplied cookie/header value.]

Mass assignment of privileged fields via workset.update(payload) — Attacker can set role/tier/approved to arbitrary privileged values by including them in the request body, bypassing intended business-logic gating. [verified: workset.update(payload) merges arbitrary attacker JSON directly onto a dict containing role/tier/approved with no field allowlist, though the result is only echoed back and not persisted, limiting real-world impact.]

Use of MD5 for security-relevant digest — Digest can be reversed via rainbow tables or brute force, undermining any integrity/verification purpose [verified: MD5 is used to hash a user-supplied phrase and returned as a 'digest', a weak/broken choice for any security-relevant hashing use.]

Weak unsalted MD5 hash usage — If this digest is relied on anywhere as a verifier/token, MD5's weakness (collisions, speed) makes it brute-forceable/forgeable. [verified: Same as idx 12: unsalted MD5 used to hash user-supplied phrase for a digest/verifier purpose.]

Missing authentication on ops identity-ping endpoint — Unauthenticated attacker can invoke an internal ops endpoint that should be gated like its siblings, expanding unauthenticated attack surface [verified: acct_identity_ping_333 is the only handler missing the _wrk_gate call entirely, reachable unauthenticated, though its current functionality is limited to echoing input.]

Security headers explicitly disabled on ops endpoint — Weakens defense-in-depth against XSS for responses served through this pattern [verified: Response explicitly sets CSP to empty and X-XSS-Protection to 0, removing browser-side defenses on this endpoint.]
